In this review, we benchmark the new AMD RX 7800 XT GPU and test it against the RX 6800 XT, NVIDIA RTX 4070, RTX 4070 Ti, RX 7900 XT, RX 6700 XT, and more. The GPU  market still has last-gen options available, complicating the decision-making process for the RX 7800 XT. In some ways, compared against NVIDIA in particular (like the 4070 or horridly positioned 4060 Ti 16GB), the 7800 XT looks strong. In others, mostly against AMD's own products (like the 6800 XT), the 7800 XT still reflects the modern trend of up-naming cards to force a repositioning of market expectations for what a $500 card should do.

comments.text:
This is what AMD gets for screwing with their NAMING SCHEME. The REAL replacement for the 6800XT is the 7900XT, as the 6900XT was the flagship being replaced by the XTX.  The 7800XT replaces the 6800 non-XT as they both have 3840 Cores and same specs. The 7900 The GRE only complicates things, as I guess it's basically 6850 non XT (but with more cores instead of Overclock)???? lol

7900 GRE Version basically offer better ray tracing, making it more competitive with Nvidia's offering, see Digital Foundry's coverage of the 7900GRE. Being as I have th 6800 non XT my only options to provide a big enough difference to REALLY notice without a frame counter, are the 7900 XTX (maybe the 7900XT) and 4080/4090. I have a 4K TV and 1440p monitor and go between them for gaming, but my 6800 still crushes most games I play at high refresh rates at 1440p, and older games as well at 4K, like prey. I'm also surprised by how well it can ray trace considering the day one reviews came out when there was like 5 games with RT. But I can play Control at 1080p maxed out with all RT at right around 60fps average, and I can play with just RT reflections at 1440p over 60fps. Upgrading my CPU to the 5800X3D from the Ryzen 5 4500 (budget low cache CPU adopted from laptops) made a HUGE difference at 1080p and 1440p. Literally DOUBLED my framerate on Far Cry 5 1080p, and like 60-70% at 1440p. Even 4K had serious enough gains to notice, ESPECIALLY in the 1% lows, because bringing those up DRAMATICALLY changes the experience. It was the most effective $300 upgrade to my gaming, and overall way faster than the cheap Ryzen 5 4500. 

Side note as well, the Fluid Motion Frames are game changers in titles like Cyberpunk, Control and Dying Light where I can use most RT settings, upscale from 1080 to 1440p (except Control without Mods for FSR) and makes it feel like 60fps average as I'm actually getting way more but without frame gen I'm hovering around mid to high 40s, low 50s. The extra frames in there really adds to it. BUT, without RT my card still plays these games great. But on RE games with RT I can play 4K max with RT maxed over 60fps, I can get about 70fps in Far Cry 6 with RT reflections, as RT shadows in that game are, well, just disappointing. The 6800 and 6800XT (now that FSR 2 exists and frame gen on any DX11 or DX12 game for AMD) are really, really aging like fine wine, as they say.  I didn't buy the 3070 during the pandemic pricing madness cause it was like $1300, and got the RX6800 instead on the day it finally dropped from like over $850 to $600, which was basically MSRP as I got an AIB Sapphire Pulse model. 16GB of VRAM is gonna make this card hold up at 1080p in new games for a LONG time, especially with driver improvements. 

AMD really did a lot considering their high end cards maxed out at a 256bit bus and 512mm² die. This being the die on the 6800 through 6950XT. Think about it, the 2080ti was previously the best of the best at $1200-$1300 and then next gen AMD came out with the 6800+6800XT that are 15% and 30% faster respectively, and that's with about 50% MORE VRAM at HALF THE PRICE!!!! From day one, with no FSR/upscaling options it was a great deal. But now, it's just an absolute gem, see the multiple videos comparing the 3070 or 3070ti with the RX6800, especially after VRAM runs out on the 3070. When I bought my RX6800 instead of 3070 I thought I was having to get the "cheap" option, but it was the better option all along. I knew the 6800 beat the 3070 and 3070 ti in averages, but I was coming from Nvidia. My mind has been opened on this matter, but only if AMD keeps bringing some competition. I hope Intel actually comes through with Battlemage as well. WE NEED MORE COMPETITION!!

Okay so I need some advice choosing my next GPU upgrade. 

Im currently running a 3070 in my rig and its great, but id love to be able to play most modern games at 4k 60 as opposed to 4k 30-45. Vram is undoubtably an issue for me aswell, 8gb just isnt enough for me. My hard cap budget for a card is 800€ and il not go any higher, but its worth mentioning that im not in a hurry to spend all 800€ if theres a better bang for buck which will meet my standards. Im looking for a 500-600€ card that will give me futureproof for 2-3 years and will allow me to do 4k 60 in most games at high (not necessarily ultra) settings then im happy. Nvidia Ray-tracing would also be nice to have aswell but its not my priority.

Firstly, is it worth the upgrading in the first place? Considering the climate and FSR 3 frame generation boosting 3070 preformance, would I be better off waiting for the 50 series or next gen AMD? Is there any chance that Nvidia's low-end 50 series might reach that 4k 60 standard? More importantly will they ever lower their mid-range card prices or will I be forced to break that 800 budget every generation?

Prices for Nvidia cards have obviously sky rocketed since the 40 series.The only cards that seem approachable are the 4070 and 4070ti. DLSS 3.5 is better than FSR 3 and the extra vram and Ray-tracing all look very appealing, plus the fact that Nvidia have historically been more reliable if their reputation preceeds them.
But on the otherhand, the 7800xt is much cheaper and has better raster preformance (Yay for minecraft shaders) than the 4070 and more futureproofed levels of VRAM too. Presumably the 7000 series card will have better FSR3 compatibility, although 5700 XT and above are supposed to have access to all features at launch, so we'll see how that turns out. The 7000 series should also have slightly better ray tracing performance. If these aren't important to you then its moot. There's also the tangible benefit of having +50 watts of overhead starting from stock settings with the 7800 XT vs 6800 XT, while also slightly lowering your electricity bills.

If you're into undervolting/underclocking, the 7800 XT is a much more energy efficient card than AMD has put out recently in this performance bracket or above. One could bring it down to 200 watts under load (similar to an RTX 4070) with a fairly minimal performance loss. In addition to saving energy, this would also keep the card running cooler than stock, allowing you to set your fan curves lower so your system runs quieter. IMO this is where the real strength of the 7800 XT lies- the 6800 XT cannot be set to 200 watts under load while remaining competitive with RTX 4070 performance.

comments.text:
I see a lot of vaguely-negative thumbnails and hot-takes on the 7800 XT, but personally I'm super excited about it. Remember: despite it being almost a year after the 7900 launch, we're still on round one of chiplet-based GPUs. So when I see people saying stuff like, "AMD just re-released the 6800 XT: it's called the 7800 XT now!" I kind of roll my eyes. Yes: the performance increase from last-gen isn't much, but AMD managed to deliver:

- A completely new kind of GPU architecture
- Power efficiency gains
- Modern QOL features (encoding)
- A seriously compelling price


And last but not least, a modestly-sized card! Look at those svelte little things!

I'm personally super excited about the 7800 XT. The "but the 6800 XT is the same performance for the same price" situation won't last: the old card inventory will dry up eventually (probably soon, we can guess-- since why would AMD launch the new one before that process was mostly complete?). It's the only card we've seen this generation that offers a compelling value proposition for a mainstream high-end (1440p high settings) GPU: the only card that even came close previously was the vanilla 4070 and that has still been overpriced since it lacked any meaningful competition.

The 7800 XT is an absolute breath of fresh air IMO. I'm just kind of sad that I won't get to buy one: I had made the decision to wait for this card to release before upgrading from my old GTX 1080, but unfortunately that card died in June and I needed a replacement immediately, so I went with a 4070 because it was the best available option at the time. But if that 1080 hadn't died, I would be 100% ordering a 7800 XT right now.

I understand (kind of) why 6800-series owners are a little underwhelmed by this card (there's certainly no reason to bin a 6800 for a 7800 if you already have one), but at the same time you gotta recognize that there are a lot of people out there who play PC games who don't buy a new graphics card every generation, and the 7800 XT is literally ~*THE CARD*~ that we've all been waiting for-- some of us for many years. There's finally a GPU that delivers great 1440p performance at a price we can feel good about, with modern a modern feature-set and power efficiency to match. I'm actually thrilled with this launch: the 7800 XT is basically a 6800 / 6800 XT with all the tradeoffs (old hardware, sometimes hard to find, poor power efficiency, no features like hardware video encoding) scratched out and delivered at basically the same price. Maybe it will even force price drops on Nvidia hardware as well, for the people who thirst for RT performance. It's nothing but good news for us consumers, IMO.

Edit: from my perspective as a 1440p-enjoyer, the cards I would buy now at various market positions would be: 6700 XT ("budget"), 7800 XT ("flagship"), 7900 XT ("money no object"). There is now no Nvidia card that I would really consider: the vanilla 4070 was the only card in Nvidia's lineup that made any sense at all, and the 7800 XT has just rendered it entirely superfluous. 4070 Ti is an $800 card with no VRAM. 4080 is a great card but needs $300-400 cut off the price tag to make any sense.

Some feedback on the new graph format for %age improvement on card comparisons (offered in the spirit of making it easier for your audience to read and compare):

1) Putting the from/to cards on the graph itself rather than just in the title (it localises the context)
2) Where there are several graphs (e.g. at different resolutions) then keep left/right the same across the series
3) Perhaps consider standardising on always having the card on the review (in this case the 7800XT) on the right so it is consistent across all graphs. Otherwise the context switch back and forth is more expensive for the viewer.
4) A matter of personal preference, but when jumping generations (6800XT vs 7800XT) then always have the newer card on the right. This might conflict with (3).

Thanks for reading! I've made more than one buying decision off the back of your reviews, and your level of technical detail is most welcome!

Test_GPU   |  var(FPS_TGPU)    - 100% (or 1)
Other_GPU |  var(FPS_OGPU) - var(OGPU%)

100fps - 100%
x            - 66.7%               x = 66.7fps

100fps - 100%
x            - 150%               x = 150fps

(O_GPU has +50fps than TGPU)
100fps - 100%
150fps - x               x = 150% = 50% faster

comments.text:
The 7800 XT naming is dumb. It's a 6700 XT successor, not a 6800 XT successor. It's using a mid-sized GPU, and it's launching at a similar MSRP to what the 6700 XT launched at. 500 USD today is equivalent to around 440 USD two and a half years ago, when the 6700 XT first launched at 480 USD, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster than the 6700 XT.

It's nothing new for previous gen graphics cards to be heavily discounted in price before many of the next gen cards replace them, and for them to have equal or better performance per dollar at those prices, yet many people are arguing things like "the 7800 XT offers little to no improvement in value per dollar over the previous generation", as if AMD is supposed to give us a major improvement in value per dollar over CURRENT pricing for the already heavily discounted 6800 XT (and other various heavily discounted 6000 series cards). 

Do you need to like the price of the 7800 XT? No. It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, and you could argue that AMD does share some degree of blame for that, though certainly not most of the blame. 

If 500 is still too expensive for you, then that sucks, because the 7700 XT is not worth considering at current pricing (even though it is fairly competitive against Nvidia alternatives). The 6700 XT is currently a potentially very good option at 330 USD, but stock will probably mostly run out in less than a year, and the 7700 XT's manufacturing cost will probably prevent AMD from offering it at a genuinely good price which can compete well against the 7800 XT's value at 500 USD, and there's still going to be a big gap between the 7600 and the 7700 XT in terms of pricing and performance from AMD, and the Nvidia options in that price range are also terrible, especially the 8GB 4060 ti. The used market will be a good place to consider if you want to pay 400 USD or less for a decent graphics card, as cards like the 6800, 3080, or 6700 XT will all potentially be good options if you can find good prices for them on the used market.

comments.text:
@stevenwest1494  The 7800 XT's name is dumb, but if you properly account for inflation, as well as the very significant discounts that the 6000 series has had, the discounted prices on cards like the 6700 XT and 6800 XT have already offered a significant generational improvement over the launch MSRP pricing of those same cards, and you can't expect the 7800 XT to offer a significant improvement over those discounted prices weren't available until more than two years after the launch of the 6000 series. The 7800 XT uses a mid-sized GPU, and is a successor to the 6700 XT, not the 6800 XT, but it offers about a 50% improvement in value per dollar over the 6800 XT's launch MSRP if you factor in a 150 dollar price drop in addition to about 18% inflation. 

It's nothing new for previous gen cards to offer equal or better value to next gen cards because of heavy discounts.

500 USD today is equivalent to about 425 USD in 2020, when the 6800 XT first launched at 650 USD, which is equivalent to about 770 USD today, which is about what you can buy the 6800 XT's true successor for (the 7900 XT).

Many people are arguing things like "the 7800 XT offers little to no improvement in value per dollar over the previous generation", as if AMD is supposed to give us a major improvement in value per dollar over CURRENT pricing for the already heavily discounted 6800 XT (and other various heavily discounted 6000 series cards). 

Do you need to like the price of the 7800 XT? No. It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, and you could argue that AMD does share some degree of blame for that, though certainly not most of the blame. 

The 4070 is also somewhat underrated because people are failing to account for the higher than normal inflation that we've had over the past three years, and despite it having less Vram, which definitely is a disadvantage, DLSS is better than FSR, and the 4070 does have significantly better power efficiency, which is always going to come with a price premium, whether you like it or not, especially when the box says Nvidia on it. The better ray tracing performance of the 4070 should not be seen as very important, relevant, or practical, but it's also still a nice-to-have if nothing else. Advantage in productivity are totally irrelevant for most people, but that's obviously a huge advantage if you actually care about it, though there are still some productivity workloads which AMD GPUs are better at. 

If 500 is still too expensive for you, then that sucks, because the 7700 XT is not worth considering at current pricing (even though it is fairly competitive against Nvidia alternatives). The 6700 XT is currently a potentially very good option at 330 USD, but stock will probably mostly run out long before the next generation comes out, and the 7700 XT is simply too close in manufacturing cost to the 7800 XT for AMD to ever want to give us a genuinely good deal on them. AMD definitely left a big gap between the 7600 (which is itself still over-priced at most retailers), and the 7800 XT, basically forcing people to buy previous gen, or used cards, if they want a good value lower-mid-range or upper-low-end graphics card, and Nvidia has also basically done the same thing, by offering poor value for everything other than the RTX 4070 (and the 4090 is arguably a good value as well, at least as far as ultra high-end cards go, but it's simply not going to be worth buying for the vast majority of gamers).

comments.text:
The 7800 XT naming is dumb. It's a 6700 XT successor, not a 6800 XT or 6800 successor. It's using a mid-sized GPU, and it's launching at a similar MSRP to what the 6700 XT launched at. 500 USD today is equivalent to around 440 USD two and a half years ago, when the 6700 XT first launched at 480 USD, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster than the 6700 XT. Of course, that launch MSRP for the 6700 XT was bloated because of the GPU shortage, but even if it had launched around 400-430 (which is likely what AMD had originally been planning), the 7800 XT would still be offering a fairly significant improvement in value over that hypothetical launch MSRP, though certainly not amazing.

It's nothing new for previous gen graphics cards to be heavily discounted in price before many of the next gen cards replace them, and for them to have equal or better performance per dollar at those prices, yet many people are arguing things like "the 7800 XT offers little to no improvement in value per dollar over the previous generation", as if AMD is supposed to give us a major improvement in value per dollar over CURRENT pricing for the already heavily discounted 6800 XT (and other various heavily discounted 6000 series cards). 

Do you need to like the price of the 7800 XT? No. It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, and you could argue that AMD does deserve some degree of the blame for that, though certainly not most of the blame. 

If 500 is still too expensive for you, then that sucks, because the 7700 XT is not worth considering at current pricing (even though it is fairly competitive against Nvidia alternatives). The 6700 XT is currently a potentially very good option at 330 USD, but stock will probably mostly run out in less than a year, and I suspect that the manufacturing cost of the 7700 XT is likely to stop AMD from wanting to offer a genuinely compelling price for it. AMD definitely left a big gap between the 7600 (which is itself still over-priced at most retailers), and the 7800 XT, basically forcing people to buy previous gen, or used cards, if they want a good value card for 400 or less, and Nvidia is also pushing us to buy upper mid-range by offering weaker value on everything below the 4070.

comments.text:
​@syncmonism Pretty much, yeah. The name is pretty irrelevant. Like Steve said, it's just marketing. What is relevant is the price to performance, which is pretty good on this card. It's not only inflation but the inceeasingly obvious diminishing returns that silicon transistor improvements are seeing. We are quickly approaching the limits of physics in silicon transistors. 
This means that R&D costs increase at a compounding rate. The same number of CUs on a newer node would necessarily be more expensive. Consumers are valuing affordability above raw performance. Sure, AMD could have turned this thing into a monster, but that would also mean getting blasted by critics for releasing another expensive GPU. Alternatively, people are going to complain about the performance and disregard the performance to cost ratio. It's a damned if you do, damned if you don't scenario. The only way to please everybody, it seems, is to adopt a financially unsustainable business model. 
Here's my takeaway: they managed to use fewer compute units to produce slightly more performance at the only really competitively priced current generation price to performance ratio. They've creatively kept costs in check by improving performance in memory and per core via architectural improvements rather than the usual AMD method of dumping electricity into it as fast as possible and yelling "POWWWWERRRRR!!!!"
I'd buy it.

comments.text:
The 7800 XT naming is dumb. It's a 6700 XT successor, not a 6800 XT successor. It's using a mid-sized GPU, and it's launching at a similar MSRP to what the 6700 XT launched at. 500 USD today is equivalent to around 440 USD two and a half years ago, when the 6700 XT first launched at 480 USD, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster than the 6700 XT.

It's nothing new for previous gen graphics cards to be heavily discounted in price before many of the next gen cards replace them, and for them to have equal or better performance per dollar at those prices, yet many people are arguing things like "the 7800 XT offers little to no improvement in value per dollar over the previous generation", as if AMD is supposed to give us a major improvement in value per dollar over CURRENT pricing for the already heavily discounted 6800 XT (and other various heavily discounted 6000 series cards). 

Do you need to like the price of the 7800 XT? No. It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, and you could argue that AMD does share some degree of blame for that, though certainly not most of the blame. 

If 500 is still too expensive for you, then that sucks, because the 7700 XT is not worth considering at current pricing (even though it is fairly competitive against Nvidia alternatives). The 6700 XT is currently a potentially very good option at 330 USD, but stock will probably mostly run out long before the next generation comes out, and the 7700 XT is simply too close in manufacturing cost to the 7800 XT for AMD to ever want to give us a genuinely good deal on them. AMD definitely left a big gap between the 7600 (which is itself still over-priced at most retailers), and the 7800 XT, basically forcing people to buy previous gen, or used cards, if they want a good value lower-mid-range or upper-low-end graphics card, and Nvidia has also basically done the same thing, by offering poor value for everything other than the RTX 4070 (and the 4090 is arguably a good value as well, at least as far as ultra high-end cards go, but it's simply not going to be worth buying for the vast majority of gamers).

comments.text:
The 7800 XT naming is dumb. It's a 6700 XT successor, not a 6800 XT successor. It's using a mid-sized GPU, and it's launching at a similar MSRP to what the 6700 XT launched at. 500 USD today is equivalent to around 440 USD two and a half years ago, when the 6700 XT first launched at 480 USD, and the 7800 XT is about 43% faster than the 6700 XT.

It's nothing new for previous gen graphics cards to be heavily discounted in price before many of the next gen cards replace them, and for them to have equal or better performance per dollar at those prices, yet many people are arguing things like "the 7800 XT offers little to no improvement in value per dollar over the previous generation", as if AMD is supposed to give us a major improvement in value per dollar over CURRENT pricing for the already heavily discounted 6800 XT (and other various heavily discounted 6000 series cards). 

Do you need to like the price of the 7800 XT? No. It sucks that average incomes haven't kept pace with inflation, and you could argue that AMD does share some degree of blame for that, though certainly not most of the blame. 

If 500 is still too expensive for you, then that sucks, because the 7700 XT is not worth considering at current pricing (even though it is fairly competitive against Nvidia alternatives). The 6700 XT is currently a potentially very good option at 330 USD, but stock will probably mostly run out long before the next generation comes out, and the 7700 XT is simply too close in manufacturing cost to the 7800 XT for AMD to ever want to give us a genuinely good deal on them. AMD definitely left a big gap between the 7600 (which is itself still over-priced at most retailers), and the 7800 XT, basically forcing people to buy previous gen, or used cards, if they want a good value lower-mid-range or upper-low-end graphics card, and Nvidia has also basically done the same thing, by offering poor value for everything other than the RTX 4070 (and the 4090 is arguably a good value as well, at least as far as ultra high-end cards go, but it's simply not going to be worth buying for the vast majority of gamers).

In anycase the 6800xt is nearly fully out of stock so its not overally relevant.
